teaser: The world's most famous kiss shows two people who are about to be murdered.
review_notes:
IMAGE: the photo appears to show a plaster (or tinted plaster) version of The Kiss, smaller and rougher in surface than the large marble in the Musee Rodin; composition is the same. Spots describe only what this view shows. The book in Paolo's hand is not visible from this angle and is only mentioned in text.
Marble commissioned by the French state in 1888, shown publicly in 1898; height about 1.8 m.
Rodin calling it 'a large sculpted knick-knack following the usual formula': quote reported in the literature, paraphrased.
Chicago 1893: a bronze of The Kiss judged unfit for general display and kept in a separate room, visible on request.
Lewes (England) 1914: the marble commissioned by Edward Perry Warren was draped with a sheet in the town hall; now at Tate.
Barbedienne foundry sold several hundred reduced bronzes (around 300).
Whether the lips actually touch is debated; the lesson only says the faces are hidden.

lesson.text: Who starts this kiss, him or her? Decide before you read on. Most people answer too fast, because they assume the answer. The sculpture has a more interesting one.

The pair have names. They are Paolo and Francesca, real people from thirteenth-century Italy. Francesca was married to Paolo's brother. One day the two were reading a love story together, the tale of Lancelot and Guinevere, and they stopped reading. Her husband found them and killed them both.

The poet Dante met their souls in his Inferno, in the circle of hell reserved for lovers. That is why Rodin modeled them, around 1882: they were meant for his great bronze doors, The Gates of Hell. In Paolo's far hand, hidden from this angle, he still holds the forgotten book.
Back to the question. One hand in this embrace is not sure of itself. Which one?

spots.title: His hand
spots.text: His large hand lies on her hip with the fingers spread and flat, hardly pressing. He sits upright, almost stiff. He is the one who hesitates.

lesson.text: Now follow her arm at the top: it is hooked around his neck, pulling his head down to hers, and her whole body leans into him. She leads. In the 1880s, showing a woman as an equal and willing partner in desire was not expected, and many viewers noticed it.
A bronze version sent to the 1893 world's fair in Chicago was judged unfit for the general public. It was put in a separate room, and visitors had to apply for permission to see it.

Rodin soon saw that the couple did not belong on the Gates. Everyone else on those doors is falling, writhing or grieving. These two are happy. He took them off and exhibited the group by itself, and critics who knew nothing of Dante simply called it The Kiss.

In 1888 the French state ordered a marble larger than life, about 1.8 meters high (6 feet). It took ten years. Like most sculptors of his day, Rodin modeled in clay and employed skilled carvers to translate the model into stone, then directed the finishing himself.
Rodin was oddly cool about his biggest crowd-pleaser. He described it as a large sculpted knick-knack made according to the usual formula, and preferred his rougher, stranger works.

He may have been unfair to himself. Walk around the group and you never get a full view of the faces. There is no single front. The story is told by backs, arms, hands and feet, which is exactly what you can inspect now.

spots.title: Hidden faces
spots.text: The two heads merge into one mass, and her arm covers his cheek. Rodin withholds the expressions, so the kiss stays private even in a museum.

spots.title: Her arm
spots.text: Her forearm wraps around the back of his neck and draws him down. This is the gesture that sets the whole group in motion.

spots.title: His back and shoulder
spots.text: Broad, upright, the muscles standing out. Compared with her curve, his torso is a wall. Rodin contrasts a body that yields with one that holds back.

spots.title: Tangled legs
spots.text: Her leg is slung over his thigh. From here it takes a moment to sort out whose limb is whose, and that confusion is part of the point.

spots.title: Her feet
spots.text: Her feet dangle off the ground, toes loose. She has given her full weight to him and to the rock.

spots.title: His foot
spots.text: His toes press into the base, taking the weight of both bodies. He is the anchor.

spots.title: The rough rock
spots.text: The seat is left scored with tool marks while the skin is smoothed. The bodies seem to be emerging from raw matter, an effect Rodin learned from Michelangelo's unfinished statues.

lesson.text: That contrast between polished flesh and unworked stone became a signature of Rodin's. It reminds you that the lovers were once inside a block, and it makes the skin look softer by comparison.

In 1914 a marble version was lent to the town hall of Lewes, in England, where soldiers were billeted. Local worthies feared it would overexcite them, and the statue spent the loan hidden under a sheet.

The public never shared Rodin's doubts. A Paris foundry sold several hundred small bronze copies for mantelpieces, and the image spread to postcards, films and advertising. Almost none of those buyers knew they were looking at two souls on their way to hell. Does knowing it change the kiss for you?

quiz.question: Who are the two lovers?
options: Paolo and Francesca, from Dante's Inferno
quiz.explanation: They are Paolo and Francesca, killed by her husband, whom Dante placed in hell.

quiz.question: Which gesture shows that the woman leads the kiss?
options: Her arm hooked around his neck, pulling him down
quiz.explanation: Her arm draws his head to hers while his hand barely presses on her hip.

quiz.question: Why did Rodin remove the couple from The Gates of Hell?
options: The state refused to pay for them
Their happiness did not fit among the suffering figures
quiz.explanation: Every other figure on the doors is in torment; these two are happy.

quiz.question: What happened to a bronze version at the 1893 Chicago world's fair?
options: It was kept in a separate room, seen only on request
quiz.explanation: It was judged unfit for the general public.

quiz.question: Why is the rock left rough?
options: So the smooth bodies seem to emerge from raw matter
The carvers ran out of time
quiz.explanation: The contrast makes the skin look softer and recalls the block the figures came from.

facts.text: Rodin considered The Kiss his greatest and most daring work.
facts.explanation: He called it a large sculpted knick-knack made by the usual formula.

facts.text: In the story, the lovers were reading a book together before they kissed.
facts.explanation: They were reading the tale of Lancelot and Guinevere, and Paolo still holds the book.

facts.text: The man's hand grips the woman's hip firmly.
facts.explanation: His hand lies flat and hesitant, hardly pressing.
